name: Greek
scriptNote: Greek alphabet. The romanised line follows the sound, not the letters; 'th' as in thin, 'dh' as in this, 'gh' a soft throat sound, 'kh' as in loch.

phrases.note: Kaliméra stretches well past noon; kalispéra takes over from mid-afternoon.
Say 'énan freddo espresso' in summer and you will pass for a local.
Shortened to 'yamas' among friends.

phrases.en: One ticket to the centre, please
phrases.local: Ένα εισιτήριο για το κέντρο, παρακαλώ
phrases.say: EH-na ee-see-TEE-ree-o ya to KEN-dro, pa-ra-ka-LO
phrases.roman: Éna eisitírio gia to kéntro, parakaló

phrases.note: The informal one. Geia sas to strangers, elders and anyone behind a counter.

phrases.en: Have a good evening (as you leave)
phrases.note: Kalispéra when you arrive, kaló vrády when you leave.
Mondays only, and everyone says it.
On the first of the month, to everyone, all day.
You will hear it at every door. The reply is 'kalós sas vríkame', roughly 'good to find you'.

phrases.en: Good to be here (the reply to welcome)

phrases.note: Said to the next table as you pass, and to you by the waiter.
Literally 'nothing': the reply to thank you.
Half a minute, which in Greece is a flexible unit.
Thank you and bless you in one. To strangers, 'na 'ste kalá'.
Birthdays, name days, every feast. The reply is 'epísis', likewise.
Stis plus the number. At one o'clock is 'sti mía'.
One syllable, two throat sounds in a row. Take it slowly.
Métrio is medium sweet, skéto no sugar, glykó sweet. Freddo is the summer coffee of Greece.
Boiled in a bríki, grounds and all. Do not drink the last sip.
Literally 'for outside'. 'Edó' for here.
Fish is priced by the kilo. Ask to see it, and ask the price before it reaches the grill.

phrases.en: Half a kilo of house wine
phrases.note: House wine comes by the kilo, in a tin jug. Chýma means loose, from the barrel.

phrases.en: Tap water is fine, thank you

phrases.note: The kérasma is serious. Refuse twice out of politeness, never a third time.
Followed by anything: échete neró, échete Wi-Fi, échete metritá.
The laïkí, the street market, sells by the kilo and shouts.

phrases.en: Which bus goes to the centre?

phrases.note: Ask before the taxi moves. The meter, 'to taxímetro', should be on.

phrases.en: What time does the ferry leave?
Can you show me on the map?
phrases.local: Μπορείτε να μου δείξετε στον χάρτη;
phrases.say: bo-REE-teh na moo DHEEK-se-teh ston KHAR-tee
phrases.roman: Boreíte na mou deíxete ston chárti

phrases.local: Ποιος είναι ο κωδικός του Wi-Fi;
phrases.say: pyos EE-neh o ko-dhee-KOS too wi-fi
phrases.roman: Poios eínai o kodikós tou Wi-Fi

phrases.en: Can I leave my bags here?
phrases.local: Μπορώ να αφήσω τις βαλίτσες εδώ;
phrases.say: bo-RO na a-FEE-so tees va-LEE-tses e-DHO
phrases.roman: Boró na afíso tis valítses edó

phrases.local: Μπορώ να έχω άλλη μία πετσέτα;
phrases.say: bo-RO na EH-kho A-lee MEE-a pe-TSEH-ta
phrases.roman: Boró na écho álli mía petséta

phrases.en: The key to room ten, please
phrases.local: Το κλειδί για το δέκα, παρακαλώ
phrases.say: to klee-DHEE ya to DHEH-ka, pa-ra-ka-LO
phrases.roman: To kleidí gia to déka, parakaló

phrases.en: What time do we have to leave the room?
phrases.local: Τι ώρα πρέπει να αφήσουμε το δωμάτιο;
phrases.say: tee O-ra PREH-pee na a-FEE-soo-meh to dho-MA-tee-o
phrases.roman: Ti óra prépei na afísoume to domátio

phrases.en: Is it safe to swim here?
I'd like to rent a scooter

phrases.note: Say it and watch the whole table warm up.

phrases.en: How do you say … in Greek?

phrases.note: The green cross. One is always on night duty, 'dianykterévon'.

phrases.en: Can I charge my phone here?
phrases.local: Μπορώ να φορτίσω το κινητό μου εδώ;
phrases.say: bo-RO na for-TEE-so to kee-nee-TO moo e-DHO
phrases.roman: Boró na fortíso to kinitó mou edó

phrases.note: To someone older or behind a desk: 'pós sas léne'.
Literally 'I was glad'. The reply is 'ki egó', me too.
Apó to Londíno, apó tin Anglía, apó ti Roumanía.

phrases.en: It's my first time in Greece
phrases.local: Είναι η πρώτη μου φορά στην Ελλάδα
phrases.say: EE-neh ee PRO-tee moo fo-RA steen e-LA-dha
phrases.roman: Eínai i próti mou forá stin Elláda

phrases.en: Shall we go for a coffee?
phrases.note: A Greek coffee lasts two hours. That is the point.

phrases.local: Μπορείτε να μου προτείνετε μια ταβέρνα;
phrases.say: bo-REE-teh na moo pro-TEE-ne-teh mya ta-VER-na
phrases.roman: Boreíte na mou proteínete mia tavérna

phrases.local: Τι αξίζει να δούμε εδώ γύρω;
phrases.say: tee a-KSEE-zee na DHOO-meh e-DHO YEE-ro
phrases.roman: Ti axízei na doúme edó gýro

phrases.note: 'Ta léme' alone is 'see you', the everyday goodbye.
The national tempo, and the answer to 'when?'
Literally 'come'. Answers the phone, voices disbelief, urges you on: one word, twenty meanings.
Literally 'in order'. Agreement, acknowledgement, resignation.
'What does it say?', between friends. The answer is 'óla kalá'.
Literally 'a joy'. How you are, how the food was, how the room is.

phrases.en: Enjoy the rest of your day
phrases.note: 'Good continuation': the shopkeeper's goodbye.
'Health to us'. Clink low and look them in the eye.
Said to the one who leaves: 'na páte sto kaló'.
A dropped plate, a near miss, a dance, a toast: the interjection for everything.
'Ánte geia' is 'bye then'. Alone it is get a move on, or disbelief.
The national shrug.
A polite, formal yes. Also 'I see', when someone explains at length.
Untranslatable: honour, duty and generosity in one word. Praise someone's filótimo and you have a friend.
Softens or sharpens anything. Strictly for people you know: 'éla re' is 'oh come on'.
Literally 'aren't you bored?'. Means never mind, don't bother.
From June on, as a goodbye.
